code.title: Mini injector: tokens, factories, cached instances

followUps:
A token is the key you ask for; a provider is the recipe that says how to produce the value for that key. A token is usually a class or an InjectionToken, and the provider pairs it with useClass, useValue, useFactory or useExisting.

Example: { provide: API_URL, useValue: 'https://api.example.test' }. Here API_URL is the token and the whole object is the provider. When a class is listed alone, as in providers: [Logger], it is shorthand for { provide: Logger, useClass: Logger }.

On its own, @Injectable() only marks the class so Angular's compiler records the types of its constructor parameters; it does not register the service anywhere. Without providedIn nobody can create it until you list it in some providers array.

If you inject it without providing it, you get NullInjectorError: No provider for X. The decorator is also needed if the class has dependencies of its own; a class with no constructor parameters can often work without it, but adding it is the safe habit. With providedIn: 'root' it also becomes a tree-shakable root singleton.

Provide it at component level when each component instance needs its own private copy of the state. Typical cases are a form-state service for one editor, a table component that keeps its own sort and page state, or a dialog with its own controller.

Example: two data grids on one page. If a GridState service is in root, both grids share one page number and fight each other. With providers: [GridState] on the grid component, each grid gets a fresh instance, and it is destroyed with the component, so nothing leaks between visits.

Because providedIn: 'any' creates a separate instance in every lazy-loaded module injector, so a service looks like a singleton but silently becomes several copies depending on how the app is split. Standalone and route-based apps no longer have that module boundary, so the option has little meaning there.

It was deprecated in favour of clear choices: 'root' for one shared instance, or a providers entry on a route or component when you want a scoped one. Predictable scope is easier to reason about than a hidden per-module copy.

An injection context is the short period during which Angular has set a "current injector" and is running your code, so inject() knows where to look. It is active in constructors and field initializers of DI-created classes, provider factories, functional guards, resolvers and interceptors, app initializers, and inside runInInjectionContext.

It is synchronous: once the function returns or you hit an await, the pointer is cleared. Code in ngOnInit, click handlers or timers is not in an injection context.

Call inject() early, in a field initializer, and keep the result; use that reference in the handler. If you need to create something dynamically, store the Injector and run the late code with runInInjectionContext.

private injector = inject(Injector);
onClick() {
  runInInjectionContext(this.injector, () => {
    const http = inject(HttpClient);
  });
}

Usually the simpler fix is private http = inject(HttpClient); as a field and then this.http in the handler.

code.title: Injector hierarchy with self, skipSelf and optional

followUps:
Content projection follows the template where the component is written, not where it is displayed. A projected component is created as a child of the component whose template declares it, so its element injector chain goes through that declaring parent.

Example: <tabs><my-panel/></tabs> written in PageComponent. my-panel can inject providers of tabs (it is content inside it) but not its viewProviders, which belong only to the tabs' own view. That is the reason viewProviders exists.

Use Angular DevTools in the browser: the component tree shows each node's providers, and the Injector Tree view shows element and environment injectors. In code you can inspect with ng.getInjector($0) in the console on a selected element in dev mode.

In your own code, injecting Injector and calling injector.get(TOKEN, null) tells you what resolves at that level, and comparing === between two lookups shows if you share one instance. A console.log in the service constructor shows how many are created.

code.title: useClass, useValue, useFactory and useExisting

followUps:
Then the two tokens give you two different objects, which usually breaks the point of the alias. With useClass, Angular constructs a new instance for the second token; with useExisting it hands back the instance already registered for the first.

Example: { provide: AuditLogger, useClass: Logger } makes a second Logger with its own state, so a log buffer is split in two. { provide: AuditLogger, useExisting: Logger } makes AuditLogger and Logger the same object, so one buffer. For NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR, a new instance would be a different component than the one on screen.

Once per injector that holds the provider: the first time the token is requested there, the result is cached, and later requests return the cached value. A component-level factory runs once per component instance; a root one runs once for the app.

Example: useFactory: () => ++count in root gives 1 on every injection. Put it in component providers and three component instances give 1, 2, 3. If you need a new value on every call, return a function from the factory and call that function instead.

Write a function that takes the config and returns EnvironmentProviders (or a provider array), built with makeEnvironmentProviders, so users only call one thing in their app config.

export function provideAcme(cfg: AcmeConfig) {
  return makeEnvironmentProviders([
    { provide: ACME_CONFIG, useValue: cfg },
    AcmeClient,
  ]);
}

Users write providers: [provideAcme({ key: 'X' })]. Optional features can be extra arguments, like provideRouter(routes, withHashLocation()). This hides internal tokens and works for tree-shaking.

An imported constant is fixed at build time and cannot change per environment, per test, per route or per component. A token can be overridden by a provider with one line, so tests can pass a fake and a lazy route can use a different value.

Example: import { API_URL } from './env' hard-wires every service to one URL; injecting API_URL lets a test supply '/mock' and a tenant supply its own. Constants are fine for true constants (a max length of 20) that never vary.

code.title: Functional interceptor chain and ordering

followUps:
The cleanest way is HttpContext: define a token, set it on the request, and read it in the interceptor.

export const SKIP_AUTH = new HttpContextToken(() => false);
http.get(url, { context: new HttpContext().set(SKIP_AUTH, true) });
// in the interceptor
if (req.context.get(SKIP_AUTH)) return next(req);

The context travels with the request through every interceptor and survives clone. Use it instead of custom headers, which would leak to the server. Good for skip-auth, retry counts and "handle my own errors" flags.

Because catchError's callback runs later, when an error arrives, and by then the injection context is gone. Calling inject() there throws NG0203.

The fix is to call inject() at the top of the interceptor, where the context exists, and use the stored variables inside the callback.

export const errors: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => {
  const router = inject(Router);
  return next(req).pipe(catchError(e => { router.navigate(['/login']); return throwError(() => e); }));
};

Retry should sit closer to the network than the error interceptor, so it retries first and the error handler sees only the final failure. With functional interceptors, the later in the array, the closer to the backend: [errorHandler, retry].

Example: a request fails twice and succeeds on the third try. With retry inside, the user sees nothing. With retry outside, the toast would pop up twice for nothing. Retry only safe methods like GET and only for 5xx or network errors, never for 401 or 400.

Use TestBed with provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([errorInterceptor])) and provideHttpClientTesting(), plus fake Router and toast service objects. Make a request, flush an error, and assert on the fakes.

http.get('/x').subscribe({ error: () => {} });
mock.expectOne('/x').flush('no', { status: 401, statusText: 'Unauthorized' });
expect(router.navigate).toHaveBeenCalledWith(['/login']);

Also test that a 500 triggers the toast and that the error still reaches the subscriber.

Use expectOne for the first URL, flush it, and only then call expectOne for the second, because the second request does not exist until the first answer arrives.

service.load().subscribe(r => result = r);
mock.expectOne('/user').flush({ id: 7 });
mock.expectOne('/orders?user=7').flush([1, 2]);
expect(result).toEqual([1, 2]);

Calling expectOne('/orders...') before the first flush fails, which proves the ordering. Finish with mock.verify().

Provide it through the real HttpClient with the testing backend, so the interceptor runs for real. Then check what the backend saw, or how the response changed.

TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [
  provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor])),
  provideHttpClientTesting() ] });
http.get('/a').subscribe();
const req = mock.expectOne('/a');
expect(req.request.headers.get('Authorization')).toBe('Bearer T');

Alternatively call the function directly inside TestBed.runInInjectionContext with a fake next.

code.title: Why inject() needs an injection context

followUps:
Because the injection context is only active while the synchronous code is running. Code before the first await runs inside the original call, but after an await the function resumes later from the event queue, when Angular has already cleared the current injector.

async load() {
  const a = inject(A);   // fine
  await fetch(url);
  const b = inject(B);   // NG0203
}

So put every inject() call at the top, or save the Injector and use runInInjectionContext.

toSignal, effect, takeUntilDestroyed, input(), viewChild() and linkedSignal-style helpers all call inject() inside to get a DestroyRef or an Injector so they can clean up automatically. That means you must call them in an injection context, typically a field initializer.

Calling effect(...) inside ngOnInit throws NG0203. Fix: pass { injector: this.injector } as an option, or move the effect to a field or the constructor.

A case: a Dropdown component has an internal DropdownState service and users project their own content, such as a <search-box> which also injects a service called DropdownState from its own feature. With providers, the projected search box would accidentally receive the dropdown's internal one and misbehave.

With viewProviders: [DropdownState] only the dropdown's own template children see it. Projected content skips it and resolves its own, so internal implementation details stay private.

Form directives like formControlName must find the parent FormGroup directive. They inject ControlContainer with @Optional() @Host() @SkipSelf() (in inject form: { optional: true, host: true, skipSelf: true }).

skipSelf avoids finding itself, host stops the search at the current template's host so a control cannot bind to a form from a different component further up, and optional avoids an error when there is no parent. The result: a control binds only to a form in the same template.

code.title: Concurrent 401s share one token refresh

followUps:
With cookie-based sessions the browser holds the credentials, so JavaScript no longer attaches or refreshes a token. The interceptor mostly sets withCredentials: true and, if the server uses CSRF protection, adds a CSRF header (Angular's built-in XSRF handling can do this).

The 401 logic simplifies: there is no token to refresh in JS, so on 401 you just redirect to login. If the server refreshes the session with a refresh cookie, that call is made once through the same shared in-flight pattern.

Fire several requests at once with a fake backend that returns 401 for the old token, and count refresh calls. Use fakeAsync or a controlled HttpTestingController.

http.get('/a').subscribe(); http.get('/b').subscribe();
mock.expectOne('/a').flush('', { status: 401, statusText: 'x' });
mock.expectOne('/b').flush('', { status: 401, statusText: 'x' });
mock.expectOne('/auth/refresh').flush({ token: 'N' });

expectOne fails if two refresh requests exist, which proves a single refresh. Then assert both retries carry the new token.

Initializer: the app waits on a known hook, the config fetch shows up in Angular's startup, and errors can be handled by Angular, but components still must read config from a service that is "loaded" by then, and a slow request delays the first render.

Pre-bootstrap fetch in main.ts: the config is a plain value, so tokens can use useValue with no loading state, and you can render an error page if it fails. The downside is code outside Angular and no DI available while fetching. Both delay first paint by one request.

Without a reload, the app must treat tenant config as changing state. Make TENANT_CONFIG a signal or an observable held by a root service, so consumers read the current value; plain useValue objects are fixed.

Steps: fetch the new config, clear caches and stateful services (or recreate them in a new environment injector via createEnvironmentInjector), update the signal, reset the router with navigateByUrl('/'). This is harder than reloading, so many apps simply reload.

Put the shared value in a Context for the tree, create the object per scope, and pass it with a Provider at the level where you want a separate copy. A hook such as useService(Token) reads the closest one.

For lazy creation, store a factory in context and create the instance once with useMemo or useRef. Nested providers act like Angular's hierarchy: a nested Provider wins for its subtree, which matches component-level providers. You must add yourself what Angular gives free, such as caching, destruction and fallbacks to a parent.

A module-level object lives for the whole server process, not for one request. On the server, two users' requests run in the same process and would read and write the same object, so one user can see another's data.

Example: export const user = { name: '' } set during request A (Alice) and read during request B (Bob) can show Alice's name to Bob. Angular SSR gives each request its own application injector, so a service in root is a fresh instance per request. Use DI for anything that holds per-user state.
